text: Your excellency:With new discoveries and industries shaking the world, our great nation must develop internally so we can face foreign empires from a position of strength.  Lumber and steel are the twin pillars of rapid advancement.

Consequently, I reccomend constructing industry as follows:Lumber mill - capacity 4; Furniture factory - capacity 1Steel mill - capacity 4; Metalwork Factory - capacity 1Textile mill - capacity 2; Clothing factory - capacity 1

We must rapidly locate and exploit the resources of our nation.  I believe our university should educate 2 prospectors, 2 miners, and 1 engineer.  In the armory we should create 2 infantry regiments for defense.
Since a small amount of global trade is necessary, our shipyard should be ordered to build one ship of the line and two indiamen.

Your Excellency:The world, unfortunately, is a hostile place.  We need to protect ourselves adequately before engaging in foreign entanglements.  To maximize the growth of the arms industry, I reccomend constructing industry as follows:
Lumber mill - capacity 4Steel mill - capacity 4; Metalwork factory - capacity 2Textile mill - capacity 2

Our university should educate 1 engineer, 1 miner, and 1 prospector to immediately expand our iron and coal mines.  The armory should recruit 2 cavalry regiments for scouting our borders and 2 infantry regiments for close defense of the capital.
The shipyard should be ordered to build 1 frigate for showing the flag at distant ports, 1 ship of the line for protection or our home waters, and 3 traders.

Your Excellency:We must dominate world trade to gain colonies and allies.  This requires a large merchant fleet and plentiful consumer goods to sell.  Consequently, I recommend constructing industry as follows:
Lumber mill - capacity 2; Furniture Factory - capacity 1Steel mill - capacity 2; Metalwork factory - capacity 1Textile mill - capacity 4; Clothing factory - capacity 2

Since we want to maximize the production in our city, our university should educate only two workers: 1 prospector and 1 engineer.  The armory should recruit 1 artillery regiment, 1 cavalry regiment, and 2 infantry regiments for exploration and defense.
The shipyard should create 4 Indiamen, representing the largest merchant capacity we can create.

These ships represent a wide variety of early 19th century wooden merchant vessels.  Traders are fairly slow, defenseless, and have a small carrying capacity.  Their one virtue is their extremely low price.

These large slow ships transported trade goods and important passengers between Europe and the Far East. Armed with a few cannons to fend off a weak pirate, they are incapable of defending themselves against a ship of the line or a frigate.

Constructed with one deck of cannons, frigates were used as scouts, raiders, and escorts. One frigate, the 44-gun U.S.S. Constitution,  defeated two British ships during the War of 1812, earning the nickname “Old Ironsides”.

Bristling with up to 130 smoothbore cannons arranged on two or three gun decks, they were the most powerful vessels in the world until the middle of the 19th Century.  The most famous example is the H.M.S. Victory, Nelson’s flagship at Trafalgar (1805).

A paddle wheel driven by early steam engines powers this fairly large and efficient merchant vessel.  Although faster than earlier sailing vessels, these early steamers could not compete with a clipper for speed.

Early scientific studies of hull design led to the clipper ships that revolutionized world trade with their amazing speed.  Clippers are more likely than other merchant ships to run a blockade successfully or to escape from hostile fleets.

By using steam engines to drive paddle wheels, these wooden  vessels are fast scouts and commerce raiders.  Their few cannon are rifled breech loaders.  Too weak to fight in the line of battle,  they use reliable steam power to escape larger vessels.

Conservative thinking and ship instability prevented the construction of sea-going ironclads until the 1850s. The H.M.S. Warrior (1859), for example, included both sails and a screw (propeller), and was armed with both smoothbore cannons and rifled guns.

New long range guns allowed ironclad battleships to achieve command of the seas. Armed with four 80 ton guns in two huge rotating turrets, the H.M.S. Inflexible  revolutionized naval warfare and remained the strongest ship afloat throughout the 1880s.

Freighter are large steam-powered merchant vessels constructed mainly of iron. With their enormous carrying capacity,  these ships represent the most efficient means of sea transport in the nineteenth century.

Great Powers evolved armored cruisers in the late 19th century  to protect or attack merchant shipping.   Inexpensive to build, they are highly efficient.  Armored cruisers can sink  raiders or early ironclads by remaining out of their range.

Efficient steam turbines allowed dreadnoughts to boast greater speed and heavier armor. H.M.S. Dreadnought made all other battleships obsolete. Its armament of ten 12 inch guns could hit from a long range and with a heavier weight than earlier ships.

The battle cruiser was conceived as a faster version of the dreadnought.  Quite successful at protecting and raiding merchant shipping,  it is risky for a battle cruiser to engage enemy dreadnoughts due to the cruiser’s lighter armor.
Infantry regiments are armed with short range, muzzle-loading smoothbore muskets.  They are slow on the march and are strongest when firing from fortifications or entrenchments.
Cavalry regiments employ both a short range pistol and a saber.  These mounted troops are excellent scouts and can be effective when attacking unprotected or unsupported infantry.

Artillery supports the other regiments in an army, and friendly infantry or cavalry must be present to protect the guns.  Although pulled by teams of horses or mules, these heavy cannons are slower then horse artillery.
Light cannons pulled by large horse teams for speed, horse artillery may be used like artillery but has the speed necessary to accompany moving cavalry.
Untrained laborers recently emigrated to the industrializing city from the agrarian counties.  From their farm experience, they view work as cyclical with time for rest and relaxation.

Since they do not understand that the modern economy requires them to labor twelve hours a day, seven days a week, untrained workers are inefficient, rebellious, and unproductive.  Fortunately, the more recalcitrant can be conscripted into the army.

With their experience of modern industry, trained workers are disciplined and efficient.  Entire families can be put to work,  laboring nearly non-stop in the factories and mills, which is of course, of great benefit to the growing industrial power.
Efficiency: 2 x UntrainedCost: 1 squad of untrained workers + 1 unit of paper + $100Career Path: expert worker, prospector, or miner

Expert workers have learned to operate complex machines and perform important crafts and trades; they are your most productive workers and therefore essential to the city’s growth.  Hugely efficient, they are no more demanding than mere trained workers.

These men move rapidly across all terrain. They are taught to take cover and fight when not in formation.
Regular infantry regiments carry muskets and bayonets. They fight best when fortified.
Grenadier’s weapons are similar to those of the regulars, but their training allows then to inflict more damage.
Hussars are the fastest scouts in the army but should not be used to attack formed troops.
Cuirassiers spearhead attacks, but are most effective when attacking unentrenched and unsupported infantry.
Horse Artillery can be risked closer to enemy lines in immediate support of an attack.
These guns devastate their foes and demolish fortifications but their slow speed makes them vulnerable.
Unformed troops armed with long rifles, adept at using terrain for concealment.
New breechloading rifles allow these infantry to fire faster, and at longer ranges.
Guard regiments recruit only the largest and strongest soldiers.
Scouts are lightly armed and fast horsemen adept at reporting on the enemy positions and escaping when sighted.
Armed with new rapid fire carbines, these cavalry regiments devestate their foes.
With a rifled gun barrel these units are capable of firing at much longer range than earlier cannons.
These guns, while extremely slow in the field,  batter entrenchments, knock down walls, and disrupt the foe.
Mostly concealed from view, these regiments withstand the fire from the enemy quite well.
Armed with modern rifles, the infantry inflicts extraordinary damage on the attacking forces.
The firepower of the machine gun makes attacking nearly suicidal without armored units.
Mechanized Infantry is used to exploit a breakthrough created by armor. Alone, they cannot successfully attack.
Armored units are used to break the enemy line or restore a shattered line and combat an enemy breakthrough.
Large guns towed behind trucks, mobile artillery is a flexible means of inflicting a preliminary bombardment.
Railroad guns, while limited in their ability to reach the battlefield, have long range and devestating power.
Sappers are useless in hand to hand combat, but are capable of destroying fortified enemy positions.
These demolition experts use newly developed explosives to destroy enemy positions.
Saboteurs are adept at demolition, and in approaching the enemy positions secretly.

These large ships are slow and  incapable of defending themselves against a ship of the line or a frigate.
Constructed with one deck of cannons, frigates are used as scouts, raiders, and escorts.
Bristling with up to 130 smoothbore cannons arranged on two or three gun decks, the most powerful vessels in the world until ironclads are developed.
Although faster than earlier sailing vessels, these early steamers cannot compete with a clipper for speed.
Clippers are more likely than other ships to run a blockade or to escape from hostile fleets, due to their speed.
These wooden  vessels are fast scouts and commerce raiders.  Their cannon are rifled breech loaders but they are  too weak to fight in the line of battle.
Early ironclads resist the firepower of foes with armor, but carry fewer cannon than a Ship-of-the-Line.
New long range guns allow advanced ironclads to achieve command of the sea.
Freighters are large vessels constructed mainly of iron. They have an enormous carrying capacity.
Inexpensive to build, these ships are highly efficient.  Armored cruisers sink  raiders by remaining out of their range.
An all big gun warship with turbine engines, a dreadnought can sink other vessels before they move in range to return fire.
Although possesed of the guns of a dreadnought,  it is risky for a battle cruiser to engage enemy dreadnoughts due to its lighter armor.
